title: Untitled
description: Untitled signed and dated 'Adnan 14' (on the reverse) oil on canvas 30.4 x 24cm (11 15/16 x 9 7/16in). Painted in 2014
provenance: White Cube, Hong Kong, no. JJ53893. | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2015. | | Exhibited | London, White Cube, Etel Adnan, 8 October - 16 November 2014. | | | | Etel Adnan was a pioneering artist, poet, playwright and essayist, whose work is imbued with the places she lived - most notably Beirut, Paris, and the San Francisco Bay area. Although widely known for her contributions to literature, including the highly acclaimed novel Sitt Marie Rose from 1977, it is her late-blooming stellar career in the visual arts that has recently gained immense recognition, solidifying her place as a key figure in modern and contemporary art history. Adnan's later works, including the present lot Untitled from 2014 were painted from memory. Intimate in scale and meditative, four distinct sections of vibrant reds, yellow and green present the essence of a rich landscape full of depth and lyricism, despite its inherent minimalist construction. It is left to the viewer to experience the work in their own way, just as these images are filled with more than one point of inspiration for the artist. "For her, 'vision is multidimensional and simultaneous', and these (...) paintings are the meeting place for many images, coalesced into one sensorial experience." ("Inside the White Cube: Etel Adnan." White Cube. www.whitecube.com/gallery-exhibitions/etel-adnan-2014. Accessed 25 September 2024.) | | Born in 1925 in Beirut - then under French mandate - to a Syrian father and a Greek mother, she was deeply influenced by her multicultural heritage and the multiple languages spoken around her. Whilst the family language was Turkish, her mother would speak Greek with her. Arabic was forbidden and considered shameful in the in the French school she attended. Today, Adnan's work which spans multiple genres is celebrated for its exploration of themes such as exile, identity, and memory, all of which are framed by her philosophical background and profound engagement with the natural world. | | Adnan's journey into the visual arts began relatively late. She started painting in her mid-30s, using a palette knife to apply oil paint directly onto canvas. This technique became one of her hallmarks, allowing her to create vibrant, abstract landscapes characterized by bold, geometric forms and radiant blocks of colour. Her visual language was heavily influenced by her surroundings and extensive travels. The landscapes she encountered, particularly Mount Tamalpais in Northern California, which was visible from home in Sausalito, became a recurrent subject in her paintings. This mountain held a near spiritual significance for Adnan, and she often depicted it in simplified, luminous compositions that verge on abstraction. Adnan's art historical influences were diverse and ranged from Islamic art and Arabic calligraphy to modernist painters such as Paul Klee and Nicolas de Staël. However, her bold, saturated colour fields, simplified abstracted forms and deeply personal relationship with nature also recall the emotional and colouristic vibrancy of Vincent Van Gogh's oeuvre. | | Adnan's beautifully balanced composition and use of vibrant colours in this painting is a wonderful example of just one area of the artist's extensive creative output – an accomplished visual artist, novelist, and poet among many other talents. Adnan has been repositioned as a leading figure in a reappraisal of global modernism that includes female artists.

title: Painting the mountain
description: Painting the mountain signed 'Lundeberg' (lower left) oil on board 30.7 x 40.8cm (12 1/16 x 16 1/16in). Painted in 1945
provenance: The artist's private collection, Los Angeles. | Tobey C. Moss Gallery, Los Angeles (probably acquired directly from the artist by October 1981). | Private collection, US (acquired from the above on 29 September 1988). | | Exhibited | Los Angeles, Los Angeles Municipal Gallery, Helen Lundeberg: A Retrospective, 16 January - 18 February 1979, no. 5. | Los Angeles, Tobey C. Moss Gallery, Los Angeles 1920s to 1960s, October - December 1981. | Los Angeles, Tobey C. Moss Gallery, Helen Lundeberg Paintings: 1937 to 1969, 15 March - 30 April 1983, no. 3. | San Francisco, Maxwell Galleries, A Woman's Vision: California Painting into the 20th Century, 30 November 1983 - 31 January 1984. | Los Angeles, Tobey C. Moss Gallery, California, 1920–1945, 5 February - 30 March 1985, no. 22. | Washington D.C., Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Aspects of California Modernism, 1920–1950, 29 January - 26 March 1986, no. 31. | | Literature | R.L.P., 'The Galleries.' in Los Angeles Times, 1983. | H. Lundeberg, letter to the present owner dated 7 November 1988. | D. Stein, 'The Art of Helen Lundeberg, Illuminating Portraits', in Woman's Art Journal, Vol. XXVII, no. 1, Spring/Summer 2006, p. 15. | | Helen Lundeberg, born in Chicago in 1908 and later settling in Pasadena, emerged as one of the pioneering figures in Modern American art, particularly within the realm of Californian Post-Surrealism. Her artistic path began under complicated circumstances, as financial constraints prevented her from pursuing a traditional university education. Instead, with the support of a family friend, she took art classes at the Stickney Memorial School of Fine Arts in Pasadena, an institution which later evolved into the Norton Simon Museum. It was under the mentorship of her teacher and fellow artist Lorser Feitelson that Lundeberg co-founded Subjective Classicism, better known as Post-Surrealism. Feitelson would go on to become Lundeberg's husband and lifelong artistic collaborator. | | Post-Surrealism prioritised meticulously structured compositions over the more arbitrary and dreamy imagery typical of its European counterpart, negotiating a renewed relationship between the perceptual and the conceptual. Lundeberg explained this distinction in her 1934 Manifesto, stating that '[t]he new aesthetic form is subjective, an ordered, pleasurable, introspective activity; an arrangement of emotions or ideas. The pictorial elements function only to create this subjective form: either emotional or mood-entity, or intellectual or idea-entity. [...] In New Classicism alone do we find an aesthetic which departs from the principles of the decorative graphic arts to found a unique order, an integrity of subject matter and pictorial structure unprecedented in the history of art'. Lundeberg eventually departed from these strict principles, yet the contemplative essence of Post-Surrealism continued to permeate her artistic production. | | During the 1930s and 1940s, Lundeberg's artistic evolution showcased her versatility across styles, gradually transitioning to the nuanced introspection characteristic of Post-Surrealism. Major exhibitions in California during this period established her as an important figure in its burgeoning art scene. These included her first solo exhibition at the Los Angeles Stanley Rose Gallery in 1933, group exhibitions at the Fine Arts Gallery of San Diego, as well as the seminal Post-Surrealists and Other Moderns exhibition at the Stanley Rose Gallery in 1935, where the Post-Surrealists first showed as a group. She was later selected for the landmark exhibition Americans, 1942: 18 Artists from Nine States at the Museum of Modern Art in New York. By the mid-1940s, when she executed Painting the mountain, Lundeberg had developed a distinctive approach that seamlessly integrated formal composition with evocative symbolism. | | The present work is a prime example of Lundeberg's Californian Post-Surrealist period, exploring the ambiguous boundaries between reality and perception. This painting is one of a series of moody, intimate pieces created in response to the large-scale murals of the Works Progress Administration that Lundeberg was commissioned to work on at the time. These sparse, mysterious scenes depict vast deserts, desolate beaches, empty rooms and seascapes, all belonging to the same serene and eerie world. A self-described 'armchair traveller' who never left the United States, the reclusive painter was an avid reader with a vivid imagination that transported her to distant lands. | | In the present work, the artist's hand figuratively enters the canvas with her brush and paints the mountain peaks in the background with a bright orange hue, the same colour used to trace her signature in the lower left corner. In a 1988 letter to the present owner, she commented on this, writing: '[y]ou may be amused to know that all the hands which appear in my paintings of the '40s and '50s are my own: it is easy to draw my left hand and reverse it if a right hand is called for'. Because of this artistic device, already used in her 1944 Self portrait now in the Zimmerli Art Museum (New Brunswick, New Jersey, US), the present work can be read as an example of meta-painting. A self-referential approach widely used in the history of art, from the Renaissance through to the work of René Magritte (1898-1967) and M.C. Escher (1898-1972), this practice has prompted viewers to delve beyond the surface narrative and engage in a deeper dialogue about the process of artistic creation itself. Lundeberg in fact executed a pencil study of an identical scene to Painting the mountain as early as 1938, shortly after publishing her manifesto, evidence of her early and prolonged interest in this composition; the work bears the title Passing Shadows and is currently held in the Weatherspoon Museum of Art, North Carolina. | | In the present composition, a solitary green shrub in the foreground adds a fragile sense of life amidst the arid landscape. This same contrast, together with the presence of the artist's hand, appears in Poetic justice (1945) at the Oakland Museum of California, which Lundeberg considered the 'sister picture' of the present work. In both works, Lundeberg created a segment of the world in which fertile growth and desolate wasteland sit side by side, expressing her interest in the paradoxical and the metaphysical. | | Central to Lundeberg's Post-Surrealism was her deliberate arrangement of elements to provoke introspection and intellectual inquiry. Rejecting subconscious automatism, she aimed to evoke 'an ordered, pleasurable, introspective activity' in viewers, urging them to explore the layers of meaning within her work (Lundeberg quoted in D. Miller, Americans, 1942: 18 Artists from Nine States, Museum of Modern Art, New York, 1942, p. 93). As written by Henry J. Seldis: '[...] introspection is the basis of her motionless art. But the very fact that it can move us to greater awareness demonstrates that her paintings are far more than a progression of metaphorical self-portraits. The absence of people in the landscapes of her mind must be taken as an invitation for us to enter.' (H.J. Seldis, Helen Lundeberg, A Retrospective Exhibition, La Jolla Museum of Contemporary Art, La Jolla, 1971-1972). Each component of Painting the mountain contributes to a cohesive narrative that transcends mere visual representation, inviting us to explore the existential and illusory dimensions of the natural world. | | Throughout her six-decades-long career, Lundeberg's lyrical and introspective yet communicative paintings gained recognition through their inclusion in prestigious collections such as the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Her works were lauded for their enigmatic symbolism, challenging viewers to contemplate the intersections of perception, reality, and the metaphysical. By rejecting the traditional Surrealist arbitrariness and embracing structured composition and meaningful symbology, Lundeberg forged a path that emphasised the intellectual engagement and philosophical depth of visual storytelling. Demonstrating the singularity of her approach, her work has since been exhibited alongside that of other major Surrealists, including in the seminal 2012 Los Angeles County Museum of Art exhibition, In Wonderland: The Surrealist Adventures of Women Artists in Mexico and The United States. There, Lundeberg's remarkable Double portrait of the artist in time (1935, lent by the Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.) was placed prominently alongside Frida Kahlo's iconic double self-portrait, The two Fridas (1939, lent by the Museo de Arte Moderno, Mexico City). | | It is no exaggeration to state that Painting the mountain is one of the most interesting and exciting paintings by the artist to come to auction, encompassing all of the hallmarks of Lundebergs' most iconic artwork: the inclusion of her own hands within the composition, the setting of a quiet California landscape and a delicate balance of distant, eerie serenity and stark introspection. The artist herself was so fond of the present work that she kept it on the wall of her room 'just above the telephone' for several years, as she declared in the abovementioned letter. The work was acquired from the Tobey C. Moss Gallery, Lundeberg's main dealer, in 1988 and has since remained in the same distinguished American private collection. It is being offered on the auction market now for the very first time, giving collectors a rare opportunity to acquire a seminal artwork, completed at the height of Lundeberg's artistic prowess and critical acclaim. As befitting this fine provenance, owned by the same collector for close to 40 years, the original invoice will be presented to the purchaser of this artwork.

title: Portrait d'homme (peut-être Achille Richard)
description: Portrait d'homme (peut-être Achille Richard) signed 'Ch. Soutine' (lower right) oil on canvas 80.8 x 64.9cm (31 13/16 x 25 9/16in). Painted in Paris circa 1916
provenance: (Possibly) Galerie Georges Chéron, Paris (acquired directly from the artist in 1917). | Galerie Henri Bing, Paris. | Éliane Brach (née Oppenheimer) Collection, New York (acquired by 1969). | Private collection, France (by descent from the above in 1980). | Private collection, Paris (by descent from the above). | | Exhibited | (Possibly) Paris, Galerie Georges Chéron, 1917. | | Literature | P. Courthion, Soutine, peintre du déchirant, Lausanne, 1972 (illustrated pp. 21 & 175, pl. C; incorrect caption, see caption 'D'). | (Possibly) C. Giraudon, 'Soutine, ses marchands, ses mécènes', in exh. cat., Chaïm Soutine (1893-1943), l'ordre du chaos, Paris, 2012, p. 32. | | | A remarkable rediscovery, Chaïm Soutine's Portrait d'homme (peut-être Achille Richard) has not been seen in public for at least half a century. Having remained within a distinguished international family of connoisseurs for decades, the work was previously known only to scholars and experts from Pierre Courthion's seminal 1972 catalogue on the artist (P. Courthion, Soutine, peintre du déchirant, Lausanne, 1972, pp. 21 & 175). Soutine's early paintings are exceptionally scarce: the artist had a habit of tracking down his earlier works and systematically destroying those he deemed to no longer meet his exacting standards. What makes this work even more exceptional is the rarity of Soutine's portraits of his friends. He typically preferred anonymous models, as his expectations were higher when it came to portraying those in his close circle, such as his fellow painter Achille Richard, the presumed sitter for this portrait. | | Soutine moved to Paris in 1912, at a time when scores of international artists, including many others from Russia and Eastern Europe, were converging upon the French capital. The rich period of artistic activity that ensued, and the fervent exchange of ideas and styles between French and émigré artists, became known somewhat paradoxically as the École de Paris. La Ruche ('The Beehive'), a cylindrical conglomeration of artist studios in Montparnasse, became the epicentre of this movement. The low studio rent and free access to models attracted many artists who had recently emigrated to Paris with little money. Soutine was among this cohort, which also included other key Modern innovators such as Marc Chagall, Ossip Zadkine, Alexander Archipenko, Constantin Brâncuși and Diego Rivera. | | La Ruche was likely where Soutine met his friend Achille Richard (1895-1962), a figure about whom relatively little is known. Despite his evident friendships and connections with artists who would later become key figures of Modern art (including Amedeo Modigliani, Léonard Tsuguharu Foujita, Pinchus Krémègne, and Moïse Kisling), Richard's life and work are largely undocumented. Existing records and ephemera suggest that he was a painter who briefly stayed at La Ruche before being drafted into World War I in June of 1917. Upon his return to Paris at the war's end, Richard enjoyed a few successes, including exhibitions at central Modern Parisian galleries such as Leopold Zborowski and Bernheim-Jeune, in the 1920s. However, he eventually faded into obscurity, succumbing to illness and alcoholism and dying at the age of 67 in 1962. | | The present portrait likely dates from before Richard's departure for the front, around 1916. At that time, Soutine possessed little resources, working as a labourer in a Renault factory and at the Grand Palais to make ends meet. In 1914, an incurable stomach ulcer prevented him from being mobilised, despite his desire to do so. Soon after, in 1915, Soutine met Modigliani through their mutual friend, Jacques Lipchitz. The two became inseparable, and the year 1916 proved to be a pivotal period for Soutine. Soutine and Modigliani moved into the same studio in the Cité Falguière, thence commencing a rich artistic exchange, often working side by side on similar works that inspired one another and allowed both of their distinctive styles to flourish. Portrait d'homme (peut-être Achille Richard) belongs to this seminal period of fervent collaboration. Taking its cue from Modigliani's iconic imagery, the present portrait features a frontal, attenuated composition, its sitter elongated by rounded shoulders and animated with deep black, entrancing almond-shaped eyes, devoid of pupils or eyelashes. | | Crucially, Modigliani also mentored the younger Soutine during this period by way of introducing him to his trusted dealers, including Léopold Zborowski, Henri Bing and Georges Chéron. A social recluse, Soutine harboured mistrust toward Paris' commercial network of dealers and collectors, however his friend's encouragement led to early exposure and recognition among this elite. Despite the relative lack of extant archival material from this time, critics have suggested that the present work is one of the Soutine's first works exhibited in a Parisian gallery, likely having passed through Galerie Georges Chéron and Galerie Henri Bing shortly after it was painted. As such, it remains in truly excellent original condition, having escaped later amendment or even destruction by the artist. In fact, it possesses but one whisper of Soutine's tendency to re-work and modify existing compositions, in the form of a pentimento: the vague outline of a book can be observed on the table to the left, evidencing that Soutine later opted to move this element to the table on the right. In multiple respects, therefore, the present work offers a rare account of the artist's early creative process. | | Soutine's influences extended beyond his contemporaries. At this time, he studied both Old and Modern Masters with great diligence, particularly Paul Cézanne, whose influence is evident in the palette and overall structural composition of the present work, which is comparable to his Portrait of Madame Cézanne (circa 1890). Similar to Cézanne, Soutine constructs the figure's face through a juxtaposition of coloured facets and angles, flattening volumes and articulating different planes to bring shape to the two-dimensional composition. | | Soutine was also an avid visitor to the Louvre, frequenting the museum as often as possible to study the Old Masters whom he would explicitly reference throughout his career. He may have been consciously or unconsciously inspired by portraits he encountered there, such as Franciabigio's Portrait d'homme (circa 1510), which exhibits an intriguing asymmetry that resonates with Portrait d'homme (peut-être Achille Richard). | | In order to fully appreciate the significance of the present work in Soutine's oeuvre and in the definition of his artistic style, his other known portrait of the same sitter invites a particularly interesting comparison. The Portrait of Achille Richard, currently housed within the McMaster Museum of Art in Ontario, Canada, was painted around the same time as the present work. In the McMaster Museum portrait, the colour palette is markedly different, centring on the warm, healthy visage of Achille Richard, set against a colourful, variegated, bright ochre background, possibly denoting wallpaper. This stands in stark contrast to the present painting, wherein the sitter is rendered in predominantly cool tones, exuding a statuesque and ethereal aura. His blue-green complexion bleeds out into his bare surroundings. Suspended from reality, he appears to inhabit a realm between life and death. His vacant eyes, hollow cheeks and ghostly pallor enhance this morbidity, the off-white highlights on his finger joints likening him to a skeleton. | | Indeed, the subsequent years of Soutine's career would affirm his enduring fascination with flesh and anatomy, whether sanguine or decomposing. He went so far as to surround himself with animal carcasses in his studio to create his celebrated series of Boeufs écorchés ('Slaughtered oxen', circa 1925). Soutine would visit slaughterhouses to procure ox carcasses, hanging them and painting among swarms of flies and unbearable stenches, as occasionally, blood would drip through his floorboards into the homes of his hapless neighbours below. | | The present portrait is one of the earliest examples of Soutine inverting traditional aesthetic values, opting for the visceral and grotesque over the conventionally beautiful and pleasing, much like his favourite poet, Charles Baudelaire (1821-1867). In particular, Baudelaire's poem, Une Charogne ('A Carcass'), may well have inspired the overall tone of this portrait. Part of his seminal work, Les Fleurs du Mal ('The Flowers of Evil', 1861), the poem exemplifies Baudelaire's fascination with the interplay between beauty and decay, life and death, and the sublime and the grotesque. | | These same thematic tensions appear throughout Soutine's oeuvre and markedly define his visual language in the present portrait. Soutine conjures a whirlwind of lively, raw brushwork and rich, complex tonality that paradoxically brings texture and vitality to the composition's morbid elements. Pink, ochre, brown, yellow, mauve, green and blue converge and interact on the canvas. In the words of one of Soutine's greatest supporters, Élie Faure, Soutine painted 'rivers of rubies, burning brimstone, droplets of turquoise, lakes of emerald crushed with sapphires... An incredible flame that twists the depths of matter after melting its mines of gemstones. That was his genius.' (É. Faure, Soutine, Paris, 1973, p. 13). Willem de Kooning later echoed that observation, stating that 'It's [all in] the lushness of the paint [...]. [Soutine] builds up a surface that looks like a material, like a substance. There's a kind of transfiguration in his work.' (quoted in The Impact of Chaïm Soutine, exh. cat., Galerie Gmurzynska, Cologne, 2002, p. 53). | | The contrast and tension between the present work and the McMaster Museum portrait can perhaps be seen as Soutine's artistic liberation from the constraints of mimesis, the aesthetic motive of imitating reality in art. Modern artists argued that instead of merely replicating nature, they should offer their own perception and interpretation of it, a theory championed by the Expressionists. Despite the McMaster Museum's portrait being more naturalistic, the present portrait seals Soutine's allegiance to the Expressionist aesthetic and confirms his ability to breathe life into the flesh of the model, offering a psychological portrait that is more realistic and revealing than reality itself. | | Pierre Courthion, recognising the importance and quality of the present work, compared it to the McMaster Museum version which he described as 'a less assertive portrait' (P. Courthion, ibid., p. 21). It is conceivable that Courthion valued the dramatic power and psychological depth of the present portrait over that of its more restrained counterpart. Larger in format and more ambitious in composition, the present work seems likely to have been completed slightly later, serving as a more assured example heralding the distinctive style that would come to secure Soutine's centrality in the history of Modern art. Having remained within private hands for at least half a century, it is being presented to the auction market now for the very first time. |

title: Standing nude in the night with bubbles
description: Standing nude in the night with bubbles signed, inscribed and dated 'Condo 99 Standing nude in the night with bubbles' (on the reverse) oil on canvas 152.5 x 127.3cm (60 1/16 x 50 1/8in). Painted in 1999
provenance: Private collection, New York (acquired directly from the artist); their sale, Sotheby's, New York, 19 May 2017, lot 456. | Private collection; their sale, Sotheby's, Hong Kong, 28 April 2022, lot 546. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | | | "There was a time when I realized that the central focal point of portraiture did not have to be representational in any way. You don't need to paint the body to show the truth about a character." (George Condo quoted in: Anney Bonney, 'George Condo by Anney Bonney, Bomb, July 1992, Online. ) | | | George Condo has been a vanguard painter since his breakthrough in the 1980s, an associate of the disruptive East Village art scene alongside Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring. Once a studio assistant in Andy Warhol's Factory, Condo developed a visual language that was unmistakably his – a child of Picasso and comic strip vocabularies – which he termed 'Artificial Realism'. His paintings combine a studied historical sense and traditional techniques with a brazen energy that shatters subjects and picture planes, melding Cubist dynamism with exquisitely rendered bodies and monolithic sculpted forms. Through these multifaceted dialogues with art historical genres and movements, Condo creates a completely novel form of picture-making. Abstaining from the de rigueur rebelliousness that was itself a springboard for many twentieth century practitioners, Condo acknowledged and continued the work of his predecessors, from Old Masters to Modern greats. He embraces contradiction and thrives on spectacle, producing canvases that are shocking, funny, powerful, but beautiful in their complexity and subjecthood. There are few painters whose oeuvre has such international acclaim and resonance. The present work, Standing nude in the night with bubbles, comes to market now and is one of the finest examples of his prolific career. | | | | Condo's early works were significant for his dramatic and new kind of figuration that merged the representational with the abstract. Standing nude in the night with bubbles exemplifies Condo's continual exploration of the formal possibilities inherent in art historical motifs, challenging conventions and redefining expectations for the depiction of the nude in a contemporary context. His compositions and subject matter often echo a rich tapestry of historical genres, traditions and movements, drawing inspiration from renowned figures of history including old masters such as Diego Veláquez and Orazio Gentileschi, to modern masters including Pablo Picasso and William de Kooning. Drawing from these more traditional tropes and portrayals and transforming them into playful and exaggerated contexts, Condo's work both revitalises and amusingly reworks the traditions of nude painting. He weaves these stories with elements of Pop Art to create his distinctive visual language and distinguishing cast of characters within a uniquely contemporary discourse. Within Condo's fantastical universe, the ambiguous anatomical form and faceless, identity-less subject offer boundless imaginative potential, humorously revitalizing and subverting the traditional nude.   | |   | | Standing nude in the night with bubbles is a striking representation of Condo's decades-long preoccupation and formal exploration of the human figure. Diverging from his contemporaries, Condo remained committed to his unique visual language and painting style which incorporated a range of historical influences. The venerable tradition of the female nude is reinterpreted through Condo's distinct pictorial language, creating a fusion of artistic and historical elements. Ralph Rugoff aptly remarked, "Condo has explored the outer suburbs of acceptability while making pictures that, for all of their outrageous humour, are deeply immersed in memories of European and American traditions of painting" (Ralph Rugoff, 'The Mental States of America' in: Exh. Cat., London, Hayward Gallery, George Condo: Mental States, 2011, p. 11).   | |   | | In the present work, the distorted and exaggerated nude figure stands prominently, in such a way that her faceless head appears to confront the viewer; a feature reminiscent of Édouard Manet's Olympia. Her body is simplified into geometric shapes, with Condo reconfiguring the anatomy of the human figure in an unexpected and unprecedented manner. Her circular breasts sit adjacent to a long, tubular neck and her long, loose arms hang limp in a fashion that recalls an empty balloon. Oscillating between figuration and abstraction, the ambiguous figure echoes the fragmented nudes of de Kooning's Woman series, while its geometric nature also conjures the surreal architectural landscapes of Giorgio de Chirico. Yellow specks emerge from her large ears, punctuating the sky with flickering stars in an orbiting formation around her head. The bubbles that occupy the surrounding nightscape add a whimsical and surreal element to the composition, that poignantly juxtaposes the distorted nude body, generating a dreamlike and visual experience.   | |   | | George Condo's pioneering visual language has earnt him a prominent place in the art world, merging classical and modernist dimensions in line with his own unique vision. Combining humour and pathos, he successfully engages viewers with his groundbreaking explorations of the human condition, and Standing nude in the night with bubbles is no exception. The present work offers the possibility to discern the traces of his influential predecessors, especially the reverberations of Manet present throughout Condo's various stylistic phrases. His inventive approach to this seminal abstract work demands the attention of the viewer and renders the painting both visually captivating and highly thought-provoking.

title: Mire G 146 (Kowloon)
description: Mire G 146 (Kowloon) signed with the artist's initials and dated 'J.D. 83' (lower right) acrylic on paper laid on canvas 135.2 x 100.2cm (53 1/4 x 39 7/16in). Painted on 10 October 1983
provenance: The artist's estate, Paris. | Isalmina Dubuffet collection, Paris (the artist's daughter, by descent from the above). | Waddington Galleries Ltd., London. | Galerie Baudoin Lebon, Paris, no. BL 7395. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Literature | M. Loreau, Catalogue des travaux de Jean Dubuffet. Fascicule XXXVI: Mires, Paris, 1988, no. 149 (illustrated p. 71). | | | | | Predominantly self-taught, Dubuffet didn't enter the art world until he was in his forties, following a successful career as a wine merchant. From the outset, he heralded a reversal in the conventions of painting, turning to the work of children, the mentally ill and marginalised cultures to create a new aesthetic which he would come to champion. Rejecting the elitism and intellectualism that had long dominated artistic discourse, this raw and unadorned aesthetic, which came to be termed Art Brut, saw Dubuffet tackle a variety of subjects across an array of different media, from the orthodox to the unprecedented. His work was defined by his rejection of the established set of values that governed art, and throughout his creative career, he derived inspiration from individuals who chose to express themselves outside of the formal realms of training – including tattooists and graffiti artists – in his quest for an instinctive pictorial language. His oeuvre stands as a defiant rebuke to the rigid traditions of Western culture, a cri de Coeur for the liberation of artistic expression from the shackles of academic art history. He sought to liberate art from its ivory tower, to reconnect it with the spontaneous and the unvarnished. | | | | The Mire series, derived from the Spanish verb 'mirar' meaning 'to look' or 'to see', marks a significant shift in Dubuffet's artistic output. This renewed perspective saw Dubuffet's subject matter transition away from depictions of the bustling life Post-War Paris in the 1960s and 1970s, and his work became increasingly psychological and less figurative. He began to paint more permissively, generating creative ideas based on dynamisms and impulses, resulting in an emotionally charged atmosphere in his paintings. Through the lens of Art Brut, he began to delve into how people perceive subjects differently, and assign disparate meanings to different objects, colours and scenes. He expanded his use of distinct cells to isolate figures and images from any wider context or narrative. | | | The significance of these works was very quickly acknowledged; only a year after the painting was executed, pieces from the Mire series were exhibited in the French pavilion at the Venice Biennale. Shortly after Dubuffet's death in 1985, a major exhibition of his late work was held at the Galerie Nationale du Jeu de Paume in Paris. Challenging the very premise of what constituted art, his artistic rebellion extended beyond mere material and techniques, Mire G 146 (Kowloon) is a seminal example of his profound avant-garde meditations on the very nature of art itself, its potentials and possibilities, inspiring generations to come. | | | Reflecting upon his all-encompassing, comprehensive vision, Dubuffet said "I want to free myself from the old nomenclature that I was led to believe catalogued reality. I want to transport my vision of what is around us in a different register, I want to live in an alternative reality." (J. Dubuffet quoted in M. Loreau, Catalogue of Works by Jean Dubuffet, issue XXXVI: Mires, Paris, 1988, p. 98). | | | In his Mire series, Dubuffet embodies this sense of boundlessness, breaking free from the banal conventions of what he believed to be a stagnant pictorial narrative. Each piece is subtitled - in this case 'Kowloon' – a title which alludes to the Chinese walled citadel demolished in the early 90s. The bright yellow backgrounds that characterise the series evoke of the colour and aesthetic of the bright Hong Kong store signs and Mandarin procession banners, while the chaotic and arbitrary nature of the lines in the painting capture the dynamic and bustling atmosphere of the city. The title 'Mire' itself questions the act of viewing an artwork. | | | Here, figuration begins to break down, resulting in a rhythmic, and almost kaleidoscopic amalgamation of colours and forms. The whimsical and childlike dynamic of the composition in the present work, reflects Dubuffet's preoccupation with Art Brut, yet the work also exudes confidence with vigorous brushstrokes and layers of paint in intertwining patterns on a large scale, immersing the viewer in its captivating labyrinth of lines and colours. The web-like structure formed by the blue lines, adds to the complexity and textural richness of the piece, further enhancing its ambiguity. The painting employs rich primary colours and abstract forms, provoking powerful reactions in its viewers as they observe this unique and provocative melange of colour, that vibrates with a frenetic energy. His lack of premeditation in his strokes and seemingly chaotic arrangement of shapes and forms, reflect his liberation from traditional artistic conventions. Thus, each viewer's interpretation is unique, evolving over time, making Mire G 146 (Kowloon) a quintessential example of how we absorb images.

description: $ (1)(see F. & S. II.274-279) The complete set of six screenprints in unique colour combinations, 1982, on Lenox Museum Board, each signed and numbered 39/60 in pencil, printed by Rupert Jasen Smith, published by the artist, New York, with the artist's copyright red ink stamp verso , the full sheets, framed Sheet 501 x 398mm (19 3/4 x 15 5/8in)(6)
provenance: Bruce R. Lewin Gallery, New York | Private Collection, Australia | | Literature | J. Schellmann & F. Feldman, Andy Warhol Prints: A Catalogue Raisonné 1962-1987, New York, 1997, no.II.274-279 (illustrated p.122). | | The Dollar Sign is one of Andy Warhol's most recognizable and powerful images. A simple form repeated in multiple vibrant colours for maximum impact. A universal symbol of wealth and aspiration, expressing the ubiquitous desire to accumulate and spend money. | | Warhol created a series of screenprints in unique colour variations which were assembled in sets of six, each in a unique combination, so no two sets have the same selection of colours. Unlike many of his screenprint images, Warhol did not use an existing image for the dollar sign, but created his own design, inspired by images in commercial typography, an industry in which he had honed his draughtsmanship skills on his arrival in New York. | | Just as he elevated everyday items, such as the humble soup can, into artworks to be contemplated from an artistic viewpoint, so he depicts the dollar sign as an object of beauty and veneration. Warhol's fascination with the pursuit of wealth was in line with the zeitgeist of the times and these works were produced as the art market was experiencing one of its most successful decades - consumerism was king and art was regarded very much as a commodity. | | The Dollar Sign screenprints are the ultimate representation of wealth and consumption. Warhol transformed this financial symbol into an artistic image, blurring the lines between art and commerce and challenging the viewer's perception of what constitutes an artwork. They remain as popular today as when they were first produced and are inextricably linked to the artist himself.

title: Personnages
description: Personnages signed and dated 'Picasso 15.3.67. III 9.4.67. 11.4.67. 14.4.67.' (lower right) pen, brush and India ink and wash on paper 38.5 x 49.7cm (15 3/16 x 19 9/16in). Executed in Mougins between 15 March and 14 April 1967
provenance: Galerie Louise Leiris, Paris. | Private collection, South Africa (acquired from the above in February 1968). | | Literature | C. Zervos, Pablo Picasso, Vol. XXV, Oeuvres de 1965 à 1967, Paris, 1972, no. 296 (illustrated p. 131). | A. Wofsy (ed.), Picasso's Paintings, Watercolors, Drawings and Sculpture, The Sixties II, 1964-1967, San Francisco, 2002, no. 67-157 (illustrated p. 321). | | By 1967, Pablo Picasso had reached the height of his creative prowess. In the picturesque environs of his villa in Vallauris, the artist produced an astonishing number of paintings, drawings and prints, driven by an unstoppable urge to create. The resulting series constitutes a dynamic fantastical corpus of remarkable range and scope, shoring his canonisation as one of the great Modern maestros of the 20th century. Colouring his distinct approach to form, technique and perspective with a primal energy, this series succeeded in interlacing the threads of his artistic mythology and animating its complex dualities: man and beast, artist and voyeur, woman and object. | | The present work represents the narrative climax of this artistic chronicle. A thick, expansive sheet packed with characters, energy and frivolity, Personnages evokes a Bacchanalian romp which is at once humorous and deeply psychological. The elements of the scene, a confluence of moving body parts rendered with contrastingly hazy and bold textures, are placed within a vital discourse by the very lines and strokes that so vividly define them. Unhampered by a specific narrative, Picasso's characters gain their life and gravitas through these dynamic interrelationships and their shifting symbolic associations. | | The scene's protagonist is introduced to the left. He possesses the visual hallmarks of a cyclops, with his single staring eye, flat nose, thick brow, elephantine hands and scruffy beard rendered in thick strokes of black ink. He looks across the sheet toward a nude woman on the right, who meets his gaze in return, the sequential layers of her face united beneath her curly hair and betraying a psychological intensity. Their connection is amplified by the striking, self-contained eye held in the cyclops' left hand, which anchors the scene both constructively and thematically. Between them, numerous vignettes of debauchery emerge. A smirking faun crawls mischievously toward a reclining nude woman, while to its left, a bearded satyr lies back, his round paunch sprouting into two thick legs, one of which ends in a buckled shoe. Dismembered body parts, tufts of hair and heads in profile populate the scene, while to the upper centre, a faun wearing a wreath stares out at the viewer with a sly smile: a seeming invitation to join the fray. | | Invoking duality and introspection, Picasso's cyclops appears to gaze at a reflection of his own eye in a mirror, echoing Picasso's unwavering curiosity into his own soul. Mirrors are a key prop in the archetypal artist's studio, as a tool with which to execute a self-portrait, thereby examining one's inner consciousness. Indeed, the raised thumb of the cyclops also places him in the position of the artist, recalling a frequent gesture by which a painter orders the scene before them, mentally arranging its perspective and scale. | | With this symbology, Picasso echoes his contemporaneous paintings, drawings and prints, whereby he would present an artist, often on the left, gazing upon his nude female subject, typically on the right. He experimented with this formula by substituting in different male archetypes for the artist figure, including musketeers, baboons and minotaurs, each of them typified by their relentless gaze. The cyclops' visage also recalls Picasso's 'barbu' characters – rustic, bearded barbarians that appeared frequently in his ceramic work. Picasso would habitually grant his male-beast protagonists with the most privileged vantage point by which to observe the scene before them – and their seductive female counterparts – by placing them starkly in the foreground. As such, they can be interpreted as both artist and voyeur, conjuring scenes that are delineated by eroticism, humour and abstraction. | | The one-eyed protagonist presents an irony, as while his vision is hampered in terms of space and depth, we the viewers are treated to the scene's visual multitudes, and the various angles and perspectives that define it. In doing so, we become acolytes of Picasso's dogmatic principle of simultaneity, the desire to grasp reality from all directions at once. This visual quest for perfection and truth had been pioneered by Picasso with the birth of Cubism at the beginning of the 20th century. Here, it infuses the scene with a voyeuristic tone, as we are only given tantalising glimpses of the female figures' bodies. Like the cyclops, we must peek and spy through gaps and crevices to catch these fleeting views. The tenets of Cubism, the very movement Picasso drove, are transformed here into the filmic segments of an erotic fantasy. | | Further consolidating the visual imagery of the Classical world, Picasso renders the righthand female nude's torso as a column, marked by its carved vertical lines and cylindrical 'foot', which forms a halo around – and a visual pun of – the woman's feet. This could be a nod toward the Classical association of slender, decorated columns with femininity, which was espoused by Vitruvius in his famous treatise, De architectura ('On architecture', c. 30-20 B.C.). Comprising both anatomy and architecture, she also takes on the role of a caryatid, a hybrid sculpture-column observed in ancient Greek and Roman temples. While she holds and anchors the construction of the mise-en-scène, she forms a counterweight to the bulky cyclops, who is invited to worship in her figurative temple. | | The present work thereby encompasses a further primary source of inspiration for Picasso, which was his own lovers. The female nude is likely to be a stand-in for Jacqueline Roque, Picasso's final wife and muse. From her first appearance in Picasso's work in 1954 until the artist's death in 1973, Roque was ubiquitous in Picasso's work, often imbuing it with twisting threads of strength and sensuality, and of vulnerability and mystery. Remarking on this, the critic Hélène Parmelin, a friend of the couple's, wrote: '[Roque] takes the place of all the models of all the painters on all the canvases... She is that enormous nude or that delicate one, that epitome of woman or that long exposition of femininity. She is sitting, lying, standing, everywhere. She is dreaming, thinking, playing... The enormous vitality of the painter feeds on this face which is itself painting, and vice versa' (H. Parmelin, Picasso Says..., London, 1966, p. 68). | | The seeming dismemberment of her feet, overlaid upon a dynamic patchwork of characters and appendages, appears to situate these elements as drawn studies that are spontaneously woven into a harmonious composition. This betrays the immediacy and endless discovery of Picasso's creative process. Indeed, the four separate dates and annotations added to the lower right illustrate that Picasso revisited this drawing on separate occasions, allowing the idea to morph and precipitate. In doing so, he utilised a range of media and drawing techniques, resulting in the work's unique confluence of thick, bold planes of ink and delicate, sfumato areas rendered with thin strokes of pen. Grey and black wash thereupon generate gradation and chiaroscuro, shrouding the scene in a veil which grants it a dreamlike and seductive atmosphere. | | Picasso purposefully employs the weightiness and bravado of Classical forms, as well as the delicacy of traditional draughtsmanship, in order to achieve this effect. In measuring himself against the artistic traditions of the past, Picasso was consciously aligning himself with the great creators of history. The repeated male profile forms to the top of the composition echo the satirical drawings of Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), as well as of 19th century French caricaturists such as Honoré Daumier (1808-1879), adapting their timeless witty takes on class and refinement. His inclusion of satyrs and fauns, the impish followers of Dionysus, equates him with ancient Greek and Roman painters who depicted their comedic hijinks on murals and vases. | | Executed shortly after the iconic exhibition Homage to Picasso in 1966, held at the Grand Palais and Petit Palais in Paris, the present work forms a celebration of Picasso's deftness as a draughtsman as well as his confident painterly touch during this mature period of his career. Showcasing impeccable provenance, this work has been in the same private collection since it was acquired by the current owners in 1968 from Picasso's main dealer, Galerie Louise Leiris. A remarkable opportunity, this work is appearing on the auction market now for the very first time.

title: Sien's mother's house seen from the back yard
description: Sien's mother's house seen from the back yard signed 'Vincent' (lower left) pen and ink and pencil heightened with white gouache on paper 29.3 x 45.8cm (11 9/16 x 18 1/16in). Executed in The Hague in May 1882

Hübner, Moderne Kunst in den Holländischen Privatsammlungen, Leipzig, 1921 (illustrated). | J-B. de la Faille, L'Oeuvre de Vincent van Gogh, Catalogue raisonné, Dessins – Aquarelles - Lithographies, Paris & Brussels, 1928, no. 941. | W. Vanbeselaere, De Hollandsche periode (1880-1885) in het werk van Vincent van Gogh (1853-1890), Antwerp, 1937, no. 941, pp. 78, 83, 130, 131 & 408. | J-B. de la Faille, The Works of Vincent van Gogh, His Paintings and Drawings, Amsterdam, 1970, no. F 941 (illustrated p. 351). | J. Hulsker, 'Van Gogh's first and only commission as an artist', in Bulletin of the Rijksmuseum Vincent van Gogh, Vincent, Vol. IV, no. 4, 1976, no. 8 (illustrated p. 11). | J. Hulsker, The Complete Van Gogh, Paintings, Drawings, Sketches, New York, 1977, no. 146 (illustrated p. 41). | G. Pollock, Vincent van Gogh and Dutch Art, PhD dissertation, London University, 1980, p. 95 (illustrated pl. 75). | G. Pollock, 'Stark encounters: Modern life and urban work in Van Gogh's drawings of The Hague 1881-3', in Art History, Vol. VI, no. 3, September 1983, p. 343. | H. van Crimpen & M. Berends-Albert, Die brieven van Vincent van Gogh, The Hague, 1990, p. 571, no. 229 (old no. 200), p. 572-573, no. 203 (old no. 202), p. 576, no. 232 (old no. 203), p. 600, no. 242 (old no. 210). | M. van der Mast & C. Dumas (eds.), Van Gogh en Den Haag, Zwolle, 1990, no. 56 (illustrated p. 50). | J-B. de la Faille, Vincent van Gogh, The Complete Works on Paper, Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. I, Text, San Francisco, 1992, no. 941. | J-B. de la Faille, Vincent van Gogh, The Complete Works on Paper, Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. II, Plates, San Francisco, 1992, no. 941 (illustrated pl. XXX). | J. Hulsker, The New Complete Van Gogh, Paintings, Drawings, Sketches, Amsterdam, 1996, no. 146, (illustrated p. 41). | | | When Vincent van Gogh received his very first art commission in 1882, he was jubilant. Addressing his brother in an impassioned letter, he wrote, 'Theo, it is almost miraculous!', followed by two more exclamation marks (Letter 210, 11 March 1882, in The Letters of Vincent van Gogh, Van Gogh Museum & Huygens Institute, Amsterdam). His uncle Cornelis Marinus van Gogh, a gallerist and bookseller in Amsterdam, had ordered twelve small pen and ink drawings of The Hague, for 2.50 guilders each (equating to around £700 for an artist working today). A second order for six larger, more detailed compositions followed, of which the present work was a crowning achievement. However, Vincent's cousin and mentor, the prominent Hague School artist Anton Mauve (1838-1888), made a cutting remark: 'it doesn't mean anything and will be the first and last', he taunted about the commission, 'and then nobody will take an interest in you' (quoted in J. Hulsker, 'Van Gogh's first and only commission as an artist', in Bulletin of the Rijksmuseum Vincent van Gogh, Vol. IV, no. 4, p. 10). Mauve's first statement, apparently motivated by the rapid deterioration of their once close relationship, was surprisingly accurate: Vincent would receive no further commissions in the course of his tragically short yet astoundingly productive career. It also hints at a deeper tension: Vincent's involvement with Clasina Maria 'Sien' Hoornik, a woman of controversial repute, had likely been the final straw for Mauve, whose disapproval of his cousin's personal choices grew alongside their artistic differences. Despite Mauve's acerbic words proving true in the short term, his jealous dismissal of Vincent's potential would later be eclipsed by the staggering influence of Vincent's work on modern art. | | The present work marks a critical period for Vincent, in which he was crystallising the core precepts that would define his life and art. Among these was a steadfast determination to improve both as an artist and as a man – a feature also tied in with his relationship to Sien. Resilient, Vincent persevered with the project, his second offering of drawings exhibiting stronger artistic confidence and technical brilliance, with deeper personal and anecdotal layers. Despite the difficult personalities in his life – who are colourfully described in his letters, an oeuvre in their own right – this was a period of optimism and liberation for Vincent. He became endlessly inspired by the beauty of The Hague's urban and rural patchwork, as well as its bustling hoi polloi. His career trajectory, from disillusioned art dealer in London to aspiring preacher in Belgium, ultimately led him to discover his true calling as an artist, encouraged by his brother Theo, who became his unwavering supporter. After a heated argument with his father, Vincent left his family home in Etten and set up a small studio in The Hague, then a bustling cultural centre undergoing rapid expansion. | | In The Hague, Vincent took on a new form of conscious humility in his search for artistic truth. Rather than portraying the city's broad, handsome streets and elegant squares, he preferred the candid vignettes of everyday life that he encountered around his studio-apartment on the Schenkweg. He mentally filtered his wanderings and observations through a rich dialogue of artistic and literary precedent which he remarked on eloquently in his letters. Among these were Jean-François Millet's (1814-1875) rustic scenes of peasants, as well as the seventeenth-century Stadsgezicht ('cityscape') paintings by Johannes Vermeer (1632-1675) and Pieter de Hooch (1629-1684). His particular focus on socially marginal figures and the drudgery of their lives was infused with the French Realist ethics of Gustave Courbet (1819-1877), as well as the nineteenth-century novels, poetry and illustrations of the metropolitan avant-garde of Paris and London. As a wandering flâneur, Vincent pictured the fragmentary, transient cityscapes conjured by Victor Hugo (1802-1885), Émile Zola (1840-1902) and Charles Dickens (1812-1870). | | At the heart of Vincent's artistic practice during this period was drawing. His technique became more meticulous yet retained his experimental flair. In the present composition, Vincent used lead pencil for the outline, reinforcing certain elements with pen and ink and bolder pencil strokes. The typical Dutch houses framing the background exhibit some evidence that he used a ruler for straight lines, though whether he used his quadrangular grid frame to arrange the perspective of this particular drawing remains inconclusive. In any case, his harmonious web of intersecting lines is thence animated by various nuances. The garden wall surging from the right serves to warp and attenuate the space, foreshadowing the vivid spatial distortion so evocative of his psychological state in his most iconic paintings. Upon the exactitude of his linework, Vincent conjures the transience of the fleeting moment, softening his technique to generate hazy sfumato textures, as in the plumes of smoke rising from the chimneystacks. Finally, he delicately highlighted certain elements with white gouache, such as the vegetable patch and window fittings. These painterly touches guide the eye across the many moments within the moment, evoking the gentle whispers of the uncanny that would come to define his corpus. The result is a richly textured and luminous composition, heady in structure and atmosphere, executed in an assured freedom. | | The present work held profound personal significance for Vincent. Rather than selecting an urban or rustic vignette, Vincent chose a domestic setting – depicting the garden of Sien's mother. Sien was Vincent's model and domestic partner at the time. She remains an enigmatic character in the mythology of Vincent's life, with much of her identity having been defined by his art and letters, thence through the writings of historians. However, recent scholarship has sought to explore her as an individual rather than a stereotype. Born into poverty, she was a single mother who worked as a seamstress and cleaner, with periods of destitution leading her to occasional sex work. She struggled with addiction and poor health when Vincent met her, and their relationship, though fraught with difficulties, marked the only domestic stability Vincent ever experienced. | | Despite admonitions from his family — including Mauve — Vincent became a devoted protector of Sien and her two young children. They moved into a larger studio together in May 1882, and Sien continued to model for him. Like his own life, however, Sien's would end tragically and abruptly. Around a year after the completion of the present work, the cracks in their relationship would become insurmountable, with Vincent regretfully leaving the family to further pursue his freedom as an artist in Drenthe. In 1904, at the age of 54, she drowned herself in the River Scheldt, an incident disturbingly foreshadowed by her in a much earlier argument with Vincent, which Vincent recounted in a letter to Theo (Letter 379, 23-29 August 1883, in The Letters of Vincent van Gogh, op. cit.). | | Vincent's devotion to Sien stemmed from his evangelical sense of mercy and his tendency to interpret reality through artistic and literary tropes. The character of Fantine, a prostitute from Les Misérables (1862), made a profound impression on him as an emblem of truth. It is entirely possible that he saw her in Sien, along with the female figures of the British social realist painters he admired, such as Luke Fildes (1843-1927) and Frank Holl (1845-1888), which he explicitly compared her to in letters to his friends. It is no surprise, therefore, that Sien inspired a remarkable range of Vincent's early work, which balanced grittiness with sentimentality. | | The female protagonist of the present drawing has not been identified, yet her prominence both within the composition and in Vincent's life and oeuvre may well suggest that she is Sien. Placed just off-centre, she is sensitively rendered in the broken, curving lines that defined Vincent's emerging aesthetic. Though she is the boldest and most clearly defined element of the scene, she is also passive and faceless, as her perspective and inner thoughts are shielded from the viewer. The two delicately drawn butterflies fluttering just outside of her eyeline could be a symbol of the two lovers, buoyant upon the buffeting winds of life, enjoying a moment of respite between storms. Butterflies were a favourite motif of Vincent's, signifying hope and transformation. Indeed, Martin Gayford has observed that Vincent recurrently associated butterflies with prostitutes, musing on their capacity for love (M. Gayford, The yellow house, Van Gogh, Gauguin and nine turbulent weeks in Provence, Boston, 2008, p. 83). She appears to be posed at half-turn, in the brief second before delightfully spotting them. One can imagine the artist tenderly watching her from inside, sitting at the window, capturing the quiet joy of the moment. | | The present work offers a window into a pivotal chapter of Vincent's life, in which he was manifesting his most fundamental values. Within the series of works completed for his uncle Cornelis, this scene truly stands out for its personal resonance. While many of the drawings are not expressly mentioned in his letters, this work was referred to several times, along with a related drawing that is currently within the permanent collection of the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena. Recognising its significance, the present work was previously owned by Hendricus Petrus Bremmer (1871-1956), an influential art historian and dealer who championed Modern art in the Netherlands. The work's rich publication and exhibition history, including its appearance in the Royal Academy's 2010 landmark Van Gogh exhibition, further shores its presence within a prestigious lineage of scholarship and connoisseurship.

title: Femme à la toque noire (Tête de jeune femme ou Portrait de femme en buste au chapeau noir)
description: Femme à la toque noire (Tête de jeune femme ou Portrait de femme en buste au chapeau noir) signed 'Renoir.' (lower right) pastel on paper laid down on board 60.8 x 46.7cm (23 15/16 x 18 3/8in). Executed circa 1890
provenance: Galerie Durand-Ruel, Paris (acquired directly from the artist on 19 March 1890). | Galerie Tanner, Zurich (acquired from the above on 11 June 1929). | Bruno Stahl Collection, Berlin and New York. | Wildenstein & Co., Inc., New York (acquired from the above in January 1949). | Jane & Charles W. Engelhard, Jr Collection, New Jersey (acquired from the above in 1956). | Jane W. Engelhard Collection (by descent from the above); her estate sale, Christie's, New York, 4 November 2004, lot 110. | Private collection (acquired at the above sale); their sale, Sotheby's, London, 24 June 2015, lot 44. | Private collection, UK (acquired at the above sale). | | Exhibited | Paris, Galeries Durand-Ruel, Tableaux, pastels - dessins par Renoir (1841-1919), 29 November - 18 December 1920, no. 68. | Houston, Allied Arts Association in association with Wildenstein & Co., Inc., New York, Masterpieces of Painting Through Six Centuries, 16-27 November 1952, no. 66. | | Literature | G-P. & M. Dauberville, Renoir, Catalogue raisonné des tableaux, pastels, dessins et aquarelles, Vol. II, 1882-1894, Paris, 2009, no. 1442 (illustrated p. 474). | | | Pierre-Auguste Renoir's Femme à la toque noire is an exceptional example of the artist's work in pastel, with its fluid strokes and bright, shimmering colours. The son of a bespoke tailor and a dressmaker, Renoir's eye for sartorial detail informed the portraiture that played an integral role in his oeuvre, exhibited here in the young woman's striking black hat. | | The present work has noteworthy provenance. It was previously owned by Bruno Stahl, an esteemed German art collector based in Berlin. Before the outbreak of World War II, Stahl entrusted the work to the Wildenstein Gallery in Paris for safekeeping. However, during the Nazi occupation of France, the pastel, along with other works belonging to Georges Wildenstein, was confiscated by the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg (ERR). The ERR was a Nazi organization responsible for seizing cultural property, especially from Jewish collectors, across occupied Europe. Confiscated artworks were often transferred to the Jeu de Paume museum in Paris, from which they were catalogued and either distributed to Nazi officials or transported to various locations across Europe. In the case of Femme à la toque noire, it was moved from Paris to the Buxheim Monastery near Memmingen, Germany, on 15 January 1943. As the war came to an end, the artwork was recovered by Allied forces and repatriated to Paris on 28 December 1945. | | On 21 March 1947, Femme à la toque noire was restituted to Georges Wildenstein and eventually returned to its rightful owner, Stahl, who had relocated to New York after the war. Camille Pissarro's Place du Carrousel (1900), now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., was also confiscated from and returned to Stahl in similar circumstances. Both artworks represent noteworthy victories within the broader effort to return looted art to its pre-war owners, many of whom – like Stahl – were persecuted by the Nazi regime.

title: Catherine Lampert Seated
description: Catherine Lampert Seated oil on canvas 51 x 41cm (20 1/16 x 16 1/8in). Painted between 1991-1992
provenance: Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., London, no. 40603.6. | Acquired from the above by the present owner. | | Literature | W. Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2009, no. 688 (illustrated p. 316). | W. Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2022, no. 688 (illustrated p. 358). | | | Frank Auerbach is one of Britain's most distinctive and celebrated painters. An artist for whom the creation of a raw, living image made in response to the presence of a seated model has for over fifty years been a fundamental, ongoing preoccupation throughout his remarkable oeuvre. Renowned especially for his heavy application of paint that masterfully fills his compositions, Auerbach is credited with making some of the most impressive, vibrant, and intuitive portraits of the post-war years. His first exhibition was held at London's Beaux Arts Gallery in 1956 and since then his paintings have become some of the most internationally collected of living artists. | | Painted between 1991 and 1992, Catherine Lampert Seated is a vibrant portrait of Auerbach's close friend, biographer, and muse, Catherine Lampert. He first met Lampert in 1978 when she was working on his retrospective at the Hayward Gallery in London, and had conducted an extensive interview with him for the catalogue. Lampert would later become Director of the Whitechapel Gallery in 1988 before later curating Auerbach's major retrospective exhibition at the Royal Academy in 2001. Over the ensuing years, she visited his studio up to twice a week, becoming the subject of more than seventy portraits that continued the explorations initiated by his earlier muses Stella West (E.O.W.), Juliet Yardley Mills (J.Y.M.), and his wife Julia. He was profoundly influenced by artists that spanned history, from Rembrandt to Soutine, through to Giacometti and de Kooning. Therefore, it is unsurprising that art historians also became fundamental to his oeuvre, including also William Feaver, the author of the most comprehensive monograph on Auerbach to date. | | The present work is a compelling display of expressive brushwork and impasto technique featuring a vibrant amalgamation of colours and texture, with thick, layered paint that adds a sculptural quality to the composition. Seated only meters away from his easel, Lampert acknowledged how "Auerbach moves noisily around the room, looks at the painting in the mirror, turns the canvas, stands back, and then rushes up, and like darts or writing on the blackboard fairly brutally tries the next throw or cancels the previous one. He is continuously active, drawing in the air, talking to himself, hardly pausing." (Catherine Lampert, Frank Auerbach Paintings and Drawings 1954-2001, exh. cat. Royal Academy of Arts, London, 2001, p. 62).  | | His vigorous and sweeping brushstrokes create a dynamic sense of movement and energy. The application of rich impasto is particularly built up in the lower and central passages, where opulent reds, earthy browns, and vibrant yellows converge, giving the work a tactile, almost three-dimensional illusion. The head and body of Lampert are rendered in a swirling sweep of brushstrokes and accumulation of pigment, projecting dynamically from the thinner areas of paint that render the background. Lampert's facial features have been executed with almost singular strokes or daubs of the brush with every gesture, shape, and colour imbued with the essence of life. As Lampert herself asserted, the moments spent with Auerbach felt as though time was suspended; "that odd limbo, not an unpleasant state, of drifting from practical self-reminders into daydreams and unquantifiable desires." (quoted in William Feaver, Frank Auerbach, New York, 2009, p. 21).   | | | Auerbach's method of execution was methodical and perpetual, he scrapes back his paintings in progress, continuously recreating the evolving image. This process is shaped by continual, intensive observation and the gradual accumulation of empirical information. Thus, the resulting portraits are steadily infused with an inexplicable vitality. Although a largely figurative painter, Auerbach's intensive and unique style renders his portraits fundamentally abstract, and they appear to reflect the artist's emotional and psychological state as much as they do of the sitter. His technique conveys not just the physical presence of the sitter, but also a profound emotional connection, evident in the intense and intimate depiction of the subject. As William Feaver once stated, 'Auerbach's heads are conceived not as busts or cameos but as presences' (William Feaver, ibid., p. 20). | | | Frank Auerbach is widely recognised as one of the most inventive and influential painters of the post-war era. Along with his 1978 retrospective at London's Hayward Gallery, the artist was also honoured in 2015 by London's Tate Britain, in partnership with Kunstmuseum Bonn, with another major retrospective of his work. Today, his paintings reside in the prestigious permanent collections of the Tate Gallery in London, the National Portrait Gallery in London; The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York; and the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid, among many others. | | | Through brilliant colour and a faultless execution of Auerbach's charismatic and established painterly gesture, Catherine Lampert Seated carries a powerful and emotional charge. The result encapsulates a seminal exposition of the artist's thoroughly inimitable and compelling portraiture which is excitingly fresh to the market.

title: Insider IX/Weeds II
description: Insider IX/Weeds II incised with the artist's initials, dated and numbered 'AP1 1998 AMDG' and stamped with the studio reference number (on the underside) cast iron 174.5 x 49.5 x 47cm (68 11/16 x 19 1/2 x 18 1/2in). Cast in 1998, this work is artist's proof 1 from an edition of 5, plus one artist's proof
provenance: Sean Kelly Gallery, New York. | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2011. | | Exhibited | Brussels, Xavier Hufkens, Insiders and Other Recent Work, 21 January - 20 March 1999 (another number from the edition exhibited). | Wiltshire, New Art Centre Roche Court Sculpture Park, Insiders, 10 February - 22 April 2001 (another number from the edition exhibited). | Malmö, Eastern Cemetery, Who Comes – Who Leaves – Who Stays, 24 August - 27 September 2002. | Monterrey, Museo De Arte Contemporaneo, Antony Gormley, 21 November 2008 – 19 April 2009. | Mexico City, Antiguo Colegio De San Ildefonso, Antony Gormley, 20 August 2009 – 31 January 2010. | | | | Antony Gormley is an internationally acclaimed British artist who has reintroduced the body to sculpture. Insider IX/Weeds II is an exemplary work that showcases the artist's investigation into the body and its relation to how human experience is manifested internally and externally. | | As with much of his early work, Gormley's 'Insider' series began with the artist casting his own body in plaster. Each mould was then cut into around 130 cross sections and laterally reduced by 60% with the height remaining the same. In doing so, the body's volume became compressed into a form of abstraction, leaving behind a kind of trace or memory. Some later 'Insider' works were derived from female bodies as well as Gormley's first child. | | As Gormley has said of these works: | An 'Insider' is to the body what memory is to consciousness: a kind of residue, something that is left behind. It is a core rather than a skeleton. It is a way of allowing things that are internal to the body – attitudes and emotions embedded in posture or hidden by gesture – to become revealed. They are equally alien and intimate. | The idea is that the pieces carry, in concentrated form, the trace of the body and its passage through life. This has a direct relationship to pain. I see these reduced forms as antennae for a particular kind of resilience that exists within all of us, that allows us to bear suffering but is itself created through painful experience. There is no judgment about this. Their bareness is not the nakedness that reveals the flesh; it is the result of having had the flesh taken away: a loss which is not sentimentalised, but accepted. The 'Insider' tries to up the ante between being and nothingness. (Antony Gormley, statement on the 'Insider' series, published on the artist's website: https://www.antonygormley.com/works/sculpture/series/insiders.) | | Made in a durable and relatively permanent base element, iron, Gormley intends that the 'Insiders' endure in time. Equally central to the artist's thinking is that iron is found at the earth's core and so, in his words, the 'Insiders' 'are like the cooled and revealed magnetic load cores of the body'. | | Gormley continually tests the boundaries of his medium to explore the relationship between time, space and the human body. The 'Insiders', including Insider IX/Weeds II, are a significant moment in his ongoing experimentation, marking as they do his first attempt to reveal the inner core of human experience. In doing so, he brings into view something that lies within all of us. These are works that in their spindly yet strangely familiar forms suggest that what is inside each of us is a self that we would maybe rather not recognise – a kind of 'third man' or alien witness. | | Gormley's contribution to British art was recognised in 1997 when he was honoured with an OBE. In 2003 Gormley became a Royal Academician and was knighted in the New Year's Honours list in 2014. Gormley's work has been widely exhibited throughout the UK and internationally with recent exhibitions at Musée Rodin, Paris (2023); Lehmbruck Museum, Duisburg (2022); Museum Voorlinden, Wassenaar (2022); National Gallery Singapore, Singapore (2021); Royal Academy of Arts, London (2019); Delos, Greece (2019); and Uffizi Gallery, Florence (2019). Permanent public works include the Angel of the North (Gateshead, England), Another Place (Crosby Beach, England) and Inside Australia (Lake Ballard, Western Australia).
